Russy Perry Jr. wrote:
>>
Do we have any idea how many [Video Story Book carts] might be out there?
>>

Sure, the number of cartridges is known (with a very small exception).  This "Video Story Book" that sold on Ebay seems to come from one created by Mike White.  The auction lists that nine of these cartridges were made.  Doubting "facts" listed in an Ebay auction is exactly what I always do.  In this case the number created (nine) was pulled directly from the "Bally/Astrocade Game Cartridge and Hardware FAQ:"

http://www.ballyalley.com/faqs/astrocade_cart_and_hardware_faq.txt

It should be noted that this is the number that Mike White created from about 1985 sometime in the 2000's (I bought mine in 2001-- I don't own it anymore).  It's certainly possible that there are a few other carts that are out there... but there certainly are not many.  Whether or not the cartridge is one rarest released to the public is quite debatable.  It wasn't ever really released at all.  Dave Carson apparently did have Astrocade's permission to create carts after they folded, and Dave had Mike do this for him.  So, it wasn't REALLY released, and all of Mike's carts are kind of just copies... but no one treats them that way in the Astrocade community; they are highly prized.

Is the cart worth $400?  Hmm, to collectors it probably is worth that much-- probably even more.  From a player's point of view it IS interesting to try it out.  Here are the docs that Mike White created and sent out to those who bought the cart:

http://www.ballyalley.com/cart_manuals/pdf_manuals/Video_Story_Book.pdf

Try using the game with those instructions and you'd be left with NOTHING.  The game would be pretty worthless to even try loading in an emulator.  However, back in March of 2008 Richard Degler disassembled the game and made instructions for it.  The instructions are in text format.  Interesting, "Video Story Book" requires an overlay (none was ever provided or made-- which doesn't mean that one doesn't exist SOMEWHERE), but Richard does explain in his docs how to use the keypad.  Richard's docs for the cartridge are here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/cart_manuals/text_manuals/video_storybook_manual.txt

Since Richard did find the program interesting and mystery enough to disassemble it, the program obviously holds some sort of intrigue.  With how to use the game solved by Richard, that still leaves the other half of the story (yeah, pun certainly intended!): where did this game REALLY come from?  What is the history of it?  Who programmed it?  When?  For what company?  Some guesses in this area have been suggested and made over the years, but nothing that the questions has ever truly been resolved to my satisfaction.

Interested in seeing what Richard came across when he looked through the code, then check out his disassembly, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/video_storybook_%282008_03_13%29.asm

Finally, if you want to try "Video Story Book," then fire up MESS and download the ROM.  The game is part of the Astrocade ROM collection, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/cart_images/ROMs/astrocade_rom_collection.zip

When giving "Video Story Book" a try, be prepared to dig in and play around with it for awhile.  Using it doesn't come naturally, and using it in MESS is even more difficult seeing that the keypad mapping in MESS isn't logical until it's remapped.

Quite a few people have the multicart (and everyone has access to MESS): who HAS devoted some time to the game?  I can raise my hand; I tried it with Richard's instructions.  Anyone else given it a go?

Adam

12261:
Today over on an APF Yahoo group a member named Jim Gerrie pointed out that his Radio Shack MC10 game, Penguino, is an entry in a programming contest called "Retrospectiva 2012."  His entry is on this page:

http://rsp.retrocomputacion.com/retrospectiva-2012-voting-phase-basic-games/

Unlike most of these sorts of programming contests this one is for games written in BASIC.  So, I thought, "It's too bad that no one wrote a game entry for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade in AstroBASIC."  Ah, then it occurred to me-- that won't happen until the MESS emulator supports saving to tape format.  The contest doesn't explicitly say in the rules that the game must run under emulation, but it's understood that no one will be able judge your game if they can't play it.  Until tape support is added to MESS, then no one can save AstroBASIC to virtual tape and thus, us Bally folks will be left out in the cold for contests of this sort.

Any thoughts?

Adam

12266:
I'm a huge fan of Gorf. I have most of the home versions ever made, even
the quickly pulled Atari Jaguar CD homebrew. The first level is called
"Astro Battles," isn't it?  The first (Space Invaders) and third levels
(Galaxian) were basically knock-offs of other arcade games, while levels
two, four and five were slightly more original (slightly). I think any
coincidence is just finding an alternative name for the level that is
reminiscent of, but not directly copying, its inspiration. Obviously the
third level, "Galaxians," doesn't try too hard, only adding an "s." It's a
great game even in its home ports (I always loved the ColecoVision
version), but only the C-64 (via the MagicVoice) and Atari Jaguar CD
versions have the speech (and of course, MAME), which really rounds out the
package.

12273:
One thing that you can do is the "DASM" command. It will disassemble the code verbatim. It does NOT know the on board commands, so those you will have to dissamble manually as per the Dave Nutting manual. The other drawback to using the DASM command is that if you say you want the default of 8K to be dissembled, it won't stop until it gets done with the whole 8K. It is better to use the beginning and end addresses so that it will stop every page. KP gets the next page. If you get a chance to see my word processor, I did that entirely using the original Blue Ram Utility. It has oless than 10 lines of BASIC, and mose of them are extremely short.
Ken

12276:
Blue Ram BASIC 1.1 uses the area !6C20 through !6FFF for all of it's variables including various stacks. Read the Blue Ram Extended memory allocation to see where everything is. Astro BASIC uses a totally different area for it's variables. They are in the high !4000 area (past the screen area). If you want to run a machine language program in the !6000 area, but want to use the Utility to put it in, first put it at !8000. Then run TEST (a cartridge). This ends up shifting the program down to the !6000 area. Then use flip the 2K-6K switch and your program will run like a cartridge. just hit reset (as long as you have the Blue Ram in ROM mode). The problem here is that you will need to re-install the Utility each time you do this.

the Blue Ram Utility doesn't START at $6000, but it DOES reside in part
of the $6000 area (unless the tape utility starts at $6000... but I
thought it runs as a cartridge after you flip the switch-- I've only user
 that version once or twice and it's been at least twelve years since I

The
 "Fast Action Graphics" program, which follows the hybrid program in the
 Arcadian that Paul is trying to use, DOES start at $6000, so Paul's small
program should work fine.  As previously stated, I've assembled "Fast Action Graphics" and run it on the Astrocade and it absolutely DOES work as
written ("Arcadian," 2, no. 10 (Sept 17, 1980): 101-102)-- minus one small change for AstroBASIC.  The assembly
version of the program is
 here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_homebrew/fastactn.asm

This
assembly version is meant for AstroBASIC.  I modified it, as only
Bally BASIC was available in 1980 and thus it was written for BallyBASIC.  See label L601A for the address of
the interrupt routine that I changed.  As seen here:

  80:            ;L601A:  CALL    $20B0            ; Envoke the Bally BASIC original Background Processor
  81:    601A  CDFD21      L601A:   CALL    $21FD            ; Call AstroBASIC's Interrupt Routine ("BG Processor")

Line 80 is commented out and line 81 has been modified with the address of AstroBASIC's routine).

I took a look at the hybrid program, but it DOESN'T use the interrupt routine, so it would seem as if nothing needs to be changed for AstroBASIC... but that's not so.  Here is the program as written in the Arcadian:

$6000 21 6e 4e 6e 26 00 22
$6007 70 4e c9

This would be entered, as Paul has been trying to do, into the Blue Ram Utility... or, in his case, the Lil' White Ram Utility.  I used the DZ80 disassembler to check what the program is doing and I get this:


 $6000 216e4e    ld      hl,$4e6e
$6003 6e        ld      l,(hl)
$6004 2600      ld      h,$00
$6006 22704e    ld      ($4e70),hl
$6009 c9        ret

The BASIC part of the program is follows:

10 A=28672;CALL 24576;PRINT B

The tutorial in the Arcadian describes the machine language and BASIC portion of the program like this:

"The BASIC program sets up an input address in variable A and calls the machine-code program (24576=6000 hex).  The machine-code program reads a byte from the memory location given to it in A and returns the value of that byte in B where the BASIC program can access it to print it."

Here are some comments from me:

Right away, it can be seen that this program will only work correctly in Bally BASIC.  In Bally BASIC variables begin at 20078 ($4E6E).  So, A is at $4E6E.  In AstroBASIC variables are in a different area, so the program would break right away.  The BASIC program stores 28672 ($7000, if I'm converting correctly) in variable A.

Here is the ML portion again, with my comments if it is run with the above BASIC program:

 $6000 216e4e    ld      hl,$4e6e  ; Load HL with $4E6E
$6003 6e        ld      l,(hl) ; Load L with high byte of what HL points to ($70)
$6004 2600      ld      h,$00  ; Load H with 0
$6006 22704e    ld      ($4e70),hl  ; Store $0070 in variable B
$6009 c9        ret

$70 in ASCII is "F."

Now the BASIC program would print "F" when the PRINT B is done.  I'm doing this off the top of my head without my books... so I may be commenting the ML portion wrong; sorry... I'm just not a Z80 natural.  Regardless, we've learned that the program is Bally BASIC only.

It sure would have been helpful if the tutorial would tell you what to expect when the hybrid program is run.  Then again, most programs in the Arcadian never did give much information about them.  Even the games sometimes were nothing more than a program name with no docs at all.  So, the user was forced to type in the program to learn what it does.

So, Paul, try running the program in Bally BASIC and let us know the results.

Hope that this helps.

Adam

How very strange that the tutorial places the hybrid and the example machine language program starting at $6000.  The "Fast Action Graphics" program is certainly not relocatable, so I'm not sure why the program example would run at $6000 if the Utility couldn't be used to enter it there.  Or, maybe you just enter it at $8000, save it, but then load it into area $6000 from Bally BASIC?  But wait, doesn't a 4K Blue Ram only have RAM from $6000-$7000?

In the meantime, since the machine language portion of the hybrid program is SO short, it can be entered directly from Bally BASIC.  It's a bit clumsy, but it will get the job done.  The hybrid program can be entered one byte at a time using the method on page 7 of the "Z80 Mini Course," here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/Z80%20Mini%20Course/Z80%20Mini%20Course%20(1982)(Larry%20Simioni).pdf

There is NO need to combine both bytes, and then enter two-bytes at a time.  Take a look at page 7 to make sure that you know what I mean.

This is what you'd write in Bally BASIC for your loader of the hybrid program:

FOR A=24576TO 26585;PRINT A,;INPUT ""%(A);NEXT A

24576 = 33 [$6000 = $21]
24577 = 110 [$6001 = $6e]
24578 = 78 [$6002 = $4e]
24579 = 110 [$6003 = $6e]
24580 = 38 [$6004 = $26]
24581 = 0 [$6005 = $00]
24582 = 34 [$6006 = $22]
24583 = 112 [$6007 = $70]
24584 = 78 [$6008 = $4e]
24585 = c9 [$6009 = $c9]

So, for the first entry your just type 33 and GO.  Note that this was all converted quite quickly using the Windows Calculator.  You might want to double-check that I didn't make a small error (which, when entering an ML program, is the same as a large error!).

Now, I THINK that the last byte entered has to always be two bytes long, but it doesn't matter in this case since you're entering an even number of bytes.  You won't run into any possible problems (I don't think) unless your entering an odd number of bytes.

This takes care of the machine language portion.  You'd enter the BASIC program as normal.  Then, SAVE your program-- don't run it!  If there are no errors, running it won't hurt... but when was the last time that you entered a program error-free?

The ML portion is NOT saved when you save the Bally BASIC program (unless you choose to save it in screen RAM in the $4xxx area, which you could do since it's so short... but that would defeat the point of the Blue Ram example).  The ML portion needs to be saved as a string, which has been discussed on this message board... but I forget the exact procedure on how it's done.  Anyone care to point to the posting(s) that were made about this subject?

Now is it becoming clear why machine language programmers didn't want to enter their programs from BASIC?  What a pain!  The Blue Ram Utility was great if you had extra RAM or the "Machine Language Monitor" cartridge would work if you only had a standard, non-upgraded Bally Arcade/Astrocade.

How very strange that the tutorial places the hybrid and the example machine language program starting at $6000.  The "Fast Action Graphics" program is certainly not relocatable, so I'm not sure why the program example would run at $6000 if the Utility couldn't be used to enter it there.  Or, maybe you just enter it at $8000, save it, but then load it into area $6000 from Bally BASIC?  But wait, doesn't a 4K Blue Ram only have RAM from $6000-$7000?

In the meantime, since the machine language portion of the hybrid program is SO short, it can be entered directly from Bally BASIC.  It's a bit clumsy, but it will get the job done.  The hybrid program can be entered one byte at a time using the method on page 7 of the "Z80 Mini Course," here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/Z80%20Mini%20Course/Z80%20Mini%20Course%20(1982)(Larry%20Simioni).pdf

There is NO need to combine both bytes, and then enter two-bytes at a time.  Take a look at page 7 to make sure that you know what I mean.

This is what you'd write in Bally BASIC for your loader of the hybrid program:

FOR A=24576TO 26585;PRINT A,;INPUT ""%(A);NEXT A

24576 = 33 [$6000 = $21]
24577 = 110 [$6001 = $6e]
24578 = 78 [$6002 = $4e]
24579 = 110 [$6003 = $6e]
24580 = 38 [$6004 = $26]
24581 = 0 [$6005 = $00]
24582 = 34 [$6006 = $22]
24583 = 112 [$6007 = $70]
24584 = 78 [$6008 = $4e]
24585 = c9 [$6009 = $c9]

So, for the first entry your just type 33 and GO.  Note that this was all converted quite quickly using the Windows Calculator.  You might want to double-check that I didn't make a small error (which, when entering an ML program, is the same as a large error!).

First, I'm not going to keep Paul in suspense: based on his PRINT results, he did enter the first two bytes correctly!  He probably also entered the rest of the program correctly too.

No byte swapping is needed to ENTER the data... but when BASIC PRINTs a value stored in a memory location, as Paul is doing, two bytes will have to be swapped to understand it!  I should have mentioned this yesterday.  Sorry about that.

Following the conversion instructions on pages 11 and 12 of the "Z80 Mini Course" we'll see how Paul's answer is correct.  Paul said that PRINT %(24576) results with 28193.  That actually IS the correct value that he should have expected.  Confusing?  Well, only until you understand why that is the correct value.  So, we'll "translate" from hex to Bally BASIC.  Strap yourself in because here we go:

1) First, Paul inputted these two values into memory at $6000:

24576 = 33 [$6000 = $21]
24577 = 110 [$6001 = $6e]

2) Next, he used the BASIC immediate command:

PRINT %(24576)

BASIC replied with:

28193

I'm not sure what result Paul expected, but he probably scratched his head thinking it was wrong, when it was actually correct.

3) I'm not going to go into details about WHY Bally BASIC does this unusual conversion and gives you two bytes back (read pages 11 and 12 of the "Z80 Mini Course" for more explanation).  I'm going to give the cookbook method for this example.  Follow this process for this example, even if the reasoning behind it isn't understood, and it will work out:

The hex value expected at address $6000 is $216E.  Let's check if 28193 (decimal) is right:

1. Break the two byte value of $216E into two separate bytes: $21 $6E
2. Now we'll make the conversion that Bally BASIC (and AstroBASIC) makes when it reads the values and PRINTs it out.
3. Flip the two separate bytes.  So $21 $6E becomes $6E $21.
4. Now convert the values to decimal and multiply by column value and then sum the columns.  Like this:

     6 x 4096 = 24,576
     14 [$E] x 256 = 3,584
     2 x 16 = 32
     1 x 1 = 1

5. Now sum the values up.  This gives us 28,193.  However, BASIC isn't done yet.
6. BASIC next checks if 28,193 is larger than 32,767?  If yes, then BASIC subtracts 65,536, else it leaves the value alone.  In our example the value is left alone.
7. This leaves us with the value: 28,193

As strange as it may look, the two-byte value at memory location $6000 of $216E is exactly equal to 28,193.  You just had to know how to do the math.

So, is it always this complicated?  Yes.  Thankfully, some of the first BASIC programs written and published in Bally BASIC did these conversions for you.  Also, as these thread progresses it becomes more and more clear just why the "Blue Ram Utility" was so often used and cited as being such a great program.

In the meantime, since the machine language portion of the hybrid program is SO short, it can be entered directly from Bally BASIC.  It's a bit clumsy, but it will get the job done.  The hybrid program can be entered one byte at a time using the method on page 7 of the "Z80 Mini Course,"
 here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/Z80%20Mini%20Course/Z80%20Mini%20Course%20(1982)(Larry%20Simioni).pdf

There is NO need to combine both bytes, and then enter two-bytes at a time.  Take a look at page 7 to make sure that you know what I mean.

This is what you'd write in Bally BASIC for your loader of the hybrid program:

FOR A=24576TO 26585;PRINT A,;INPUT ""%(A);NEXT A

24576 = 33 [$6000 = $21]
24577 = 110 [$6001 = $6e]
24578 = 78 [$6002 = $4e]
24579 = 110 [$6003 = $6e]
24580 = 38 [$6004 = $26]
24581 = 0 [$6005 = $00]
24582 = 34 [$6006 = $22]
24583 = 112 [$6007 = $70]
24584 = 78 [$6008 = $4e]
24585 = c9 [$6009 = $c9]

So, for the first entry your just type 33 and GO.  Note that this was all converted quite quickly using the Windows Calculator.  You might want to double-check that I didn't make a small error (which, when entering an ML program, is the same as a
 large error!).

Now, I THINK that the last byte entered has to always be two bytes long, but it doesn't matter in this case since you're entering an even number of bytes.  You won't run into any possible problems (I don't think) unless your entering an odd number of bytes.

This takes care of the machine language portion.  You'd enter the BASIC program as normal.  Then, SAVE your program-- don't run it!  If there are no errors, running it won't hurt... but when was the last time that you entered a program error-free?

The ML portion is NOT saved when you save the Bally BASIC program (unless you choose to save it in screen RAM in the $4xxx area, which you could do since it's so short... but that would defeat the point of the Blue Ram example). I should have pointed out that while this is the conversion method shown in the "Z80 Mini Course," there is a faster "by hand" method to be used.  The method previously shown was just to follow the method laid out in the "Z80 Mini Course."  This is the much shorter method:

I) Convert Bally BASIC Hexadecimal to Decimal:

1. Flip the two separate bytes stored.  In the Hybrid program example at memory location $6000 is $216E.  It becomes $6E21.

2. Using a calculator (like the one included with Windows) enter $6E21 in hex and then press decimal to convert it to decimal.

3. The calculator's result is 28,193.

4. Is the result larger than 32,767?  If yes, then subtract 65,536, else leave the value alone.


II) Convert Bally BASIC positive decimal numbers to hexadecimal:

1) Convert the decimal number to hex using a calculator.  So 28,193 becomes $6E21.
2) All hex numbers must be four digits long for this process to work.  For example, if you convert 1 to hex you get $1.  You must supply the leading zeros.  $1 would become $0001.  Another example would be: 255.  This would be 255 = $FF.  Make it four digits: $00FF.
3) Flip the two separate bytes.  $6E21 becomes $216E.  Or $0001 becomes $0100.  Or $00FF becomes $FF00.

III) Convert Bally BASIC negative decimal to hexadecimal:

1) Add 65,536 to the negative decimal number.  We'll use the a very large number -2.  So, -2 + 65,536 is 65,534.
2) Convert the decimal number to hex using a calculator.  So 65,534 becomes $FFFE
3) Flip the two separate bytes.  $FFFE becomes $FEFF.

I hope this helps you to understand the conversion process and that I'm not muddying the waters.

Adam

First, I'm not going to keep Paul in suspense: based on his PRINT results, he did enter the first two bytes correctly!  He probably also entered the rest of the program correctly too.

No byte swapping is needed to ENTER the data... but when BASIC PRINTs a value stored in a memory location, as Paul is doing, two bytes will have to be swapped to understand it!  I should have mentioned this yesterday.  Sorry about that.

Following the conversion instructions on pages 11 and 12 of the "Z80 Mini Course" we'll see how Paul's answer is correct.  Paul said that PRINT %(24576) results with 28193.  That actually IS the correct value that he should have expected.  Confusing?  Well, only until you understand why that is the correct value.  So, we'll "translate" from hex to Bally BASIC.  Strap yourself in because here we go:

1) First, Paul inputted these two values into memory at $6000:

24576 = 33 [$6000 = $21]
24577 = 110 [$6001 = $6e]

2) Next, he used the BASIC immediate command:

PRINT %(24576)

BASIC replied with:

28193

I'm not sure what result Paul expected, but he probably scratched his head thinking it was wrong, when it was actually correct.

3) I'm not going to go into details about WHY Bally BASIC does this unusual conversion and gives you two bytes back (read pages 11 and 12 of the "Z80 Mini Course" for more explanation).  I'm going to give the cookbook method for this example.  Follow this process for this example, even if the reasoning behind it isn't understood, and it will work out:

The hex value expected at address $6000 is $216E.  Let's check if 28193 (decimal) is right:

1. Break the two byte value of $216E into two separate bytes: $21 $6E
2. Now we'll make the conversion that Bally BASIC (and AstroBASIC) makes when it reads the values and PRINTs it out.
3. Flip the two separate bytes.  So $21 $6E becomes $6E $21.
4. Now convert the values to decimal and multiply by column value and then sum the columns.  Like this:

     6 x 4096 = 24,576
     14 [$E] x 256 = 3,584
     2 x 16 = 32
     1 x 1 = 1

5. Now sum the values up.  This gives us 28,193.  However, BASIC isn't done yet.
6. BASIC next checks if 28,193 is larger than 32,767?  If yes, then BASIC subtracts 65,536, else it leaves the value alone.  In our example the value is left alone.
7. This leaves us with the value: 28,193

As strange as it may look, the two-byte value at memory location $6000 of $216E is exactly equal to 28,193.  You just had to know how to do the math.

So, is it always this complicated?  Yes.  Thankfully, some of the first BASIC programs written and published in Bally BASIC did these conversions for you. FOR A=24576TO 26585;PRINT A,;INPUT ""%(A);NEXT A

24578 = 78 [$6002 = $4e]
24579 = 110 [$6003 = $6e]

24581 = 0 [$6005 = $00]
24582 = 34 [$6006 = $22]
24583 = 112 [$6007 = $70]
24584 = 78 [$6008 = $4e]
24585 = c9 [$6009 = $c9]

How very strange that the tutorial places the hybrid and the example machine language program starting at $6000.  The "Fast Action Graphics" program is certainly not relocatable, so I'm not sure why the program example would run at $6000 if the Utility couldn't be used to enter it there.  Or, maybe you just enter it at $8000, save it, but then load it into area $6000 from Bally BASIC?  But wait, doesn't a 4K Blue Ram only have RAM from $6000-$7000?

In the meantime, since the machine language portion of the hybrid program is SO short, it can be entered directly from Bally BASIC.  It's a bit clumsy, but it will get the job done.  The hybrid program can be entered one byte at a time using the method on page 7 of the "Z80 Mini Course,"
 here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/Z80%20Mini%20Course/Z80%20Mini%20Course%20(1982)(Larry%20Simioni).pdf

There is NO need to combine both bytes, and then enter two-bytes at a time.  Take a look at page 7 to make sure that you know what I mean.

This is what you'd write in Bally BASIC for your loader of the hybrid program:

FOR A=24576TO 26585;PRINT A,;INPUT ""%(A);NEXT A

24576 = 33 [$6000 = $21]
24577 = 110 [$6001 = $6e]
24578 = 78 [$6002 = $4e]
24579 = 110 [$6003 = $6e]
24580 = 38 [$6004 = $26]
24581 = 0 [$6005 = $00]
24582 = 34 [$6006 = $22]
24583 = 112 [$6007 = $70]
24584 = 78 [$6008 = $4e]
24585 = c9 [$6009 = $c9]

So, for the first entry your just type 33 and GO.  Note that this was all converted quite quickly using the Windows Calculator.  You might want to double-check that I didn't make a small error (which, when entering an ML program, is the same as a
 large error!).

Now, I THINK that the last byte entered has to always be two bytes long, but it doesn't matter in this case since you're entering an even number of bytes.  You won't run into any possible problems (I don't think) unless your entering an odd number of bytes.

>I should have pointed out that while this is the conversion method shown in the "Z80 Mini Course," there is a faster "by hand" method to be used.  The method previously shown was just to follow the method laid out in the "Z80 Mini Course."  This is the much shorter method:
>
>I) Convert Bally BASIC Hexadecimal to Decimal:
>
>1. Flip the two separate bytes stored.  In the Hybrid program example at memory location $6000 is $216E.  It becomes $6E21.
>
>2. Using a calculator (like the one included with Windows) enter $6E21 in hex and then press decimal to convert it to decimal.
>
>3. The calculator's result is 28,193.
>
>4. Is the result larger than 32,767?  If yes, then subtract 65,536, else leave the value alone.
>
>
>32769 is  -32767 and 65,535 is actually -1
>
>
>II) Convert Bally BASIC positive decimal numbers to hexadecimal:
>
>1) Convert the decimal number to hex using a calculator.  So 28,193 becomes $6E21.
>2) All hex numbers must be four digits long for this process to work.  For example, if you convert 1 to hex you get $1.  You must supply the leading zeros.  $1 would become $0001.  Another example would be: 255.  This would be 255 = $FF.  Make it four digits: $00FF.
>3) Flip the two separate bytes.  $6E21 becomes $216E.  Or $0001 becomes $0100.  Or $00FF becomes $FF00.
>
>III) Convert Bally BASIC negative decimal to hexadecimal:
>
>1) Add 65,536 to the negative decimal number.  We'll use the a very large number -2.  So, -2 + 65,536 is 65,534.
>2) Convert the decimal number to hex using a calculator.  So 65,534 becomes $FFFE
>3) Flip the two separate bytes.  $FFFE becomes $FEFF.
>
>I hope this helps you to understand the conversion process and that I'm not muddying the waters.

So the Utility will reside @ !6000-!7FFF AND !E000-!FFFF changing something In the area of !E000-!FFFF will edit the Utility or allotted memory locations for BR BASIC.

Paul, to save ML code at 300-baud for Bally BASIC this is an overview of what I'd do-- it may SEEM convoluted... but once you get the work flow down then it should actually go rather quickly:

1) Type the ML code into a hex editor and save the hex (bin) file.  Or, if it's in source form, then assemble it and save the bin file.

2) Use Lance Squire's "Bin2BML" to convert the binary file to a BML file for use with Bob Colbert's "AstroWAV."

3) Use "AstroWAV" to create a binary file that would load at 2000-baud.

4) Load the created 2000-baud file into the $6000 area (or wherever it's needed) of the Blue Ram.  You MIGHT get a "question mark" load error because this is basically a string and the load might be one byte too long (or too short?).  I ran into this before when Richard Degler and I were working on archiving, "Maze Avenger," which uses a string of ML code and data.  There was a workaround, but if you need it, then I'll have to look into it again (it's a thread, as we talked about it publicly).

5) Switch the toggle switch of the 'Lil White Ram to change the RAM to ROM.

6) I'd put in the Bally BASIC cart and reset the machine (RAM in the 'Lil White Ram will be safe).  This means that there should be no need to use the "Ibach Cartridge Conversion and Cartridge Swapping Method" to swap the BASIC carts while the Astrocade is on.

7) I'd save the area of the 'Lil White Ram that holds the ML program as a string.

I THINK that this is the best method to do it.  I can't remember the exact details on how this would work, but Paul you're an Archive Jedi!, so you can figure it out-- I have faith in ya!  (And when you do get a good work flow that handles this in the best way possible, maybe you can write it up).

12292:
To answer your question about the early 4K Blue Rams, they only went from $6000 to $7FFF. There was no utility in whole. All of the utility routines were separate modules. Not until John and Clyde made the PCBs was there a 16K and later the 32K which required a lot of piggy-backing of chips.
So to answer inquisitive minds, no the Utility will not work in 4K, hand wired Blue Rams. There is no room for anything else but the Utility. I guess to could edit the $4000 area, but only with care.
Ken

To answer your question about the early 4K Blue Rams, they only went from $6000 to $7FFF. There was no utility in whole. All of the utility routines were separate modules. Not until John and Clyde made the PCBs was there a 16K and later the 32K which required a lot of piggy-backing of chips.

Paul, to save ML code at 300-baud for Bally BASIC this is an overview of what I'd do-- it may SEEM convoluted... but once you get the work flow down then it should actually go rather quickly:

1) Type the ML code into a hex editor and save the hex (bin) file.  Or, if it's in source form, then assemble it and save the bin file.

2) Use Lance Squire's "Bin2BML" to convert the binary file to a BML file for use with Bob Colbert's "AstroWAV."

3) Use "AstroWAV" to create a binary file that would load at 2000-baud.

4) Load the created 2000-baud file into the $6000 area (or wherever it's needed) of the Blue Ram.  You MIGHT get a "question mark" load error because this is basically a string and the load might be one byte too long (or too short?).  I ran into this before when Richard Degler and I were working on archiving, "Maze
 Avenger," which uses a string of ML code and data.  There was a workaround, but if you need it, then I'll have to look into it again (it's a thread, as we talked about it publicly).

5) Switch the toggle switch of the 'Lil White Ram to change the RAM to ROM.

6) I'd put in the Bally BASIC cart and reset the machine (RAM in the 'Lil White Ram will be safe).  This means that there should be no need to use the "Ibach Cartridge Conversion and Cartridge Swapping Method" to swap the BASIC carts while the Astrocade is on.

7) I'd save the area of the 'Lil White Ram that holds the ML program as a string.

 up).

OK, here is my definitive technique for making hybrid machine language/Bally BASIC programs.

1. Using a hex editor or an assembler, create a binary file for the machine language portion on your PC. Use the extension .prg.

2. Using prg2txt, convert the .prg file to a .txt file. It will look like gibberish because it's trying to translate the binary data into the BASIC character set, but that's OK.

prg2txt.exe example.prg example.txt -e -n

3. Edit the .txt file as follows. At the very top, type out the program's BASIC code using the prg2txt/txt2prg format. Immediately after the BASIC code, add the following line to load the machine language data to 24576 (6000 in hex), adding the machine code's size in bytes to 24576 to get the ending value in the FOR loop:

&(192)=0;A=24576;for N=Ato (24576 + size of machine language);%(N)=KP;next N

At the very end of the .txt file, add

:return

or

:return ;run

Remember that keywords like return and run need to have a space after them.

4.  Use txt2prg to convert the edited .txt file back to a .prg file.

txt2prg.exe example-edit.txt example-edit.prg

5.  Use KCS to create a .wav file that can be loaded into Bally BASIC with :INPUT.

KCSWIN.exe -M -L3 -P35 example-edit.prg example-edit.wav


As an example, here's my edited .txt file for the example program in Arcadian volume 2, page 100.

10 A=28672;CALL 24576;print B
&(192)=0;A=24576;for N=Ato 24586;%(N)=KP;next N
!goto Ngoto &null "return N{-55}
:return ;run

The documentation doesn't seem to be instructions for the separate "utility" programs that Ken was referring to (which Paul infers when he says, "If I have other versions, they aren't labeled as such").  I've always used Blue Ram BASIC 1.1 with the Blue Ram expansion.  I just presumed that the earlier version of the BASIC would have been similar.  Now I'm not sure if this is even an earlier version of BASIC.  It's some sort of hybrid that allows Bally BASIC to access RAM, under certain conditions, in the $6000 area (this area is normally out of reach of Bally BASIC, which is limited to the built in RAM at $4000).

Blue Ram OS 1.0 is not similar AT ALL to Blue Ram BASIC 1.1.  If you read through the "Blue Ram OS 1.0" documentation then you'll see that you would have had access to 1.8K of RAM (the screen RAM normally available to BASIC), plus another 3.8K of RAM available on the Blue Ram unit (meaning this was meant for the first Blue Ram expansions shipped).  It seems that using Blue Ram OS 1.0 would have popped you in and out of Bally BASIC and the Blue Ram OS depending on what you were doing.  This program definitely seems like a stop-gap measure so that people that bought the Blue Ram expansion would have SOME way to use it besides only programming it in machine language.  Given BASIC users access to it was a good idea, and it was eventually followed up with Blue Ram BASIC, which was a full-fledged BASIC that didn't require Bally BASIC at all.

So, would Blue Ram OS 1.0 still have saved through the 300-baud interface?

With the help of Richard Houser's Arcadian compilation tapes borrowed from Lance, I've been able to really thoroughly archive the first two volumes of The Arcadian. This was before AstroBASIC was even out, so you'd better like 300 baud! Richard's tapes covered the first couple of volumes pretty thoroughly. He included all of the big programs, but didn't always put in small programs or variations of longer programs. But once I had these, it was pretty easy to generate the alternative versions (as when Bob printed a reader suggestion for improving a program). And the short programs I just typed in and converted with the 300 baud tools for the PC.  Sometimes, Richard made small changes to the code printed in The Arcadian. I won't guarantee I caught all of these, but when I did, I've included both his modified version and the original.  The tape for volume 3 had only a small portion of the programs from this volume. As far as I know, this is all he did. I'm including all the programs from this tape that hadn't already been archived, but I haven't tried to fill in the gaps.

      With the help of Richard Houser's Arcadian compilation tapes borrowed from Lance, I've been able to really thoroughly archive the first two volumes of The Arcadian. This was before AstroBASIC was even out, so you'd better like 300 baud! Richard's tapes covered the first couple of volumes pretty thoroughly. He included all of the big programs, but didn't always put in small programs or variations of longer programs. But once I had these, it was pretty easy to generate the alternative versions (as when Bob printed a reader suggestion for improving a program). And the short programs I just typed in and converted with the 300 baud tools for the PC.  Sometimes, Richard made small changes to the code printed in The Arcadian. I won't guarantee I caught all of these, but when I did, I've included both his modified version and the original.  The tape for volume 3 had only a small portion of the programs from this volume. As far as I know, this is all he did. I'm including all the programs from this tape that hadn't already been archived, but I haven't tried to fill in the gaps.



Here's a list of what I uploaded to the FTP server (dated 5-23-2013). I haven't made notes for most of the programs, because the best source of information is probably looking them up in The Arcadian. Check Mike White's software list to find the exact locations. If I have a version of a program with comments removed, it's because the program ran out of memory as it was printed. I'm not sure why they included comment lines in this case.  A few programs require a RAM expansion, but they still just load into Bally BASIC with :INPUT.  I discovered that the Critter program we got from Mike White included some of his own modifications. I'm not sure if these were made when Critter was first published or only when he sent them to us.

12305:
I added the "Blue Ram Operating System 1.0," a program, distributed on 300-baud tape, that in conjunction with Bally BASIC allows access to the Blue Ram unit's extended RAM.  We've been discussing this Blue Ram O.S., and it's nice to be able to add this rare software to the website while it's still relevant to the current discussion.  Thanks to Paul Thacker for getting this archived and sent to me so quickly.

You can download "Blue Ram Operating System 1.0" here:

http://tinyurl.com/qa5jut9

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/misc/Blue%20RAM%20OS%201.0%20(1981)(Perkins%20Engineering).zip

Here is a little more information about the operating system:

Most users of the Blue Ram expansion unit are aware of "Blue Ram BASIC 1.1," as eventually it became Perkin Engineering's standard method to program any extended RAM beyong the original 4K that shipped with the Bally Arcade/Astrocade console. The program that first shipped on 300-baud tape allowed BASIC users to access extended memory, "Blue Ram OS 1.0," is a hybrid between Bally BASIC and newly written routines which allow access to extended RAM.

"Blue Ram OS 1.0" is not similar AT ALL to "Blue Ram BASIC 1.1." If you read through the "Blue Ram OS 1.0" documentation then you'll see that you would have had access to 1.8K of RAM (the screen RAM normally available to BASIC), plus another 3.8K of RAM available on the Blue Ram unit (meaning this was meant for the first Blue Ram expansions shipped). It seems that using "Blue Ram OS 1.0" would have popped you in and out of Bally BASIC and the Blue Ram OS depending on what you were doing. This operating system definitely seems like a stop-gap measure so that people that bought the Blue Ram expansion would have SOME way to use it besides only programming it in machine language. Giving BASIC users access to extended RAM was a great idea. This program was eventually followed up with "Blue Ram BASIC 1.1," which was a full-fledged BASIC that didn't require "Bally BASIC" at all.

The brief, 5-page instructions for this preliminary operating system for the original 4K Blue Ram expansion unit are here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/perkins/perkins_blue_ram_os_1.0.pdf

Enjoy!

Adam

With the help of Richard Houser's Arcadian compilation tapes borrowed from Lance, I've been able to really thoroughly archive the first two volumes of The Arcadian. This was before AstroBASIC was even out, so you'd better like 300 baud! Richard's tapes covered the first couple of volumes pretty thoroughly. He included all of the big programs, but didn't always put in small programs or variations of longer programs. But once I had these, it was pretty easy to generate the alternative versions (as when Bob printed a reader suggestion for improving a program). And the short programs I just typed in and converted with the 300 baud tools for the PC.  Sometimes, Richard made small changes to the code printed in The Arcadian. I won't guarantee I caught all of these, but when I did, I've included both his modified version and the original.  The tape for volume 3 had only a small portion of the programs from this volume. As far as I know, this is all he did. I'm
 including all the programs from this tape that hadn't already been archived, but I haven't tried to fill in the gaps.

Here's a list of what I uploaded to the FTP server (dated 5-23-2013). I haven't made notes for most of the programs, because the best source of information is probably looking them up in The Arcadian. Check Mike White's software list to find the exact locations. If I have a version of a program with comments removed, it's because the program ran out of memory as it was printed. I'm not sure why they included comment lines in this case.  A few programs require a RAM expansion, but they still just load into Bally BASIC with :INPUT.  I discovered that the Critter program we got from Mike White included some of his own modifications. I'm not sure if these were made when Critter was first published or only when he sent them to us.

I added the "Blue Ram Operating System 1.0," a program, distributed on 300-baud tape, that in conjunction with Bally BASIC allows access to the Blue Ram unit's extended RAM.  We've been discussing this Blue Ram O.S., and it's nice to be able to add this rare software to the website while it's still relevant to the current discussion.  Thanks to Paul Thacker for getting this archived and sent to me so quickly.

You can download "Blue Ram Operating System 1.0" here:

http://tinyurl.com/qa5jut9

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/misc/Blue%20RAM%20OS%201.0%20(1981)(Perkins%20Engineering).zip

Here is a little more information about the operating system:

Most users of the Blue Ram expansion unit are aware of "Blue Ram BASIC 1.1," as eventually it became Perkin Engineering's standard method to program any extended RAM beyong the original 4K
 that shipped with the Bally Arcade/Astrocade console. The program that first shipped on 300-baud tape allowed BASIC users to access extended memory, "Blue Ram OS 1.0," is a hybrid between Bally BASIC and newly written routines which allow access to extended RAM.

"Blue Ram OS 1.0" is not similar AT ALL to "Blue Ram BASIC 1.1." If you read through the "Blue Ram OS 1.0" documentation then you'll see that you would have had access to 1.8K of RAM (the screen RAM normally available to BASIC), plus another 3.8K of RAM available on the Blue Ram unit (meaning this was meant for the first Blue Ram expansions shipped). It seems that using "Blue Ram OS 1.0" would have popped you in and out of Bally BASIC and the Blue Ram OS depending on what you were doing. This operating system definitely seems like a stop-gap measure so that people that bought the Blue Ram expansion would have SOME way to use it besides only programming it in machine language. Giving BASIC
 users access to extended RAM was a great idea. This program was eventually followed up with "Blue Ram BASIC 1.1," which was a full-fledged BASIC that didn't require "Bally BASIC" at all.

The brief, 5-page instructions for this preliminary operating system for the original 4K Blue Ram expansion unit are here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/perkins/perkins_blue_ram_os_1.0.pdf

Enjoy!

Adam

Paul Thacker wrote:
>>
Unless I missed one, I didn't include anything that's an

>>

I didn't mean to imply that Paul had exact duplicates, just programs that are archived in SOME format or other (we've got a lot of that on BallyAlley.com).  It's not TRUE duplication, but for many of the programs most users would be hard pressed to tell the difference.

>>
some
 of these we previously had only in AstroBASIC format. Bally BASIC is
the more authentic format (though slowly loading) since this is what the
 authors used when writing these early programs.>>

For most programs the AstroBASIC version is preferred (by me) because of the slight boost in speed that AstroBASIC gives the programs when they run.  There is a big difference between some WaveMakers programs ("Lookout for the Bull" springs to mind).  However, it shuld be kept in mind that the original programmer MEANT the program to run at the speed that they did and while speed enhancements may make the program run better for ME, it may not be when the programmer intended or would EVER want.

Oftentimes the AstroBASIC programs were slightly altered when converted from Bally BASIC.  As Paul said, the 300-Baud version is certainly more authentic... if less useable by most people (since the 300-baud interface is so rare).  Also, some programs were made to work properly in AstroBASIC by modifiying the original program... and that's certainly a no-no when archiving... even if the mod was made thirty years ago.

Adam

12311:
while most 300 baud Bally BASIC programs will run in AstroBASIC, There are some programs out there that won't. However, if a program was written in ASTRO, the chances of it working in BALLY are slim. None of the scroll modes or music routines from ASTRO will work in BALLY. Also the link to the calculator that was on BALLY is not in ASTRO. There are no *() commands in BALLY, but the @() array is in both, and works identically.
Ken

>With the help of Richard Houser's Arcadian compilation tapes borrowed from Lance, I've been able to really thoroughly archive the first two volumes of The Arcadian. This was before AstroBASIC was even out, so you'd better like 300 baud! Richard's tapes covered the first couple of volumes pretty thoroughly. He included all of the big programs, but didn't always put in small programs or variations of longer programs. But once I had these, it was pretty easy to generate the alternative versions (as when Bob printed a reader suggestion for improving a program). And the short programs I just typed in and converted with the 300 baud tools for the PC.  Sometimes, Richard made small changes to the code printed in The Arcadian. I won't guarantee I caught all of these, but when I did, I've included both his modified version and the original.  The tape for volume 3 had only a small portion of the programs from this volume. As far as I know, this is all he did. I'm
 including all the programs from this tape that hadn't already been archived, but I haven't tried to fill in the gaps.
>
>Here's a list of what I uploaded to the FTP server (dated 5-23-2013). I haven't made notes for most of the programs, because the best source of information is probably looking them up in The Arcadian. Check Mike White's software list to find the exact locations. If I have a version of a program with comments removed, it's because the program ran out of memory as it was printed. I'm not sure why they included comment lines in this case.  A few programs require a RAM expansion, but they still just load into Bally BASIC with :INPUT.  I discovered that the Critter program we got from Mike White included some of his own modifications. I'm not sure if these were made when Critter was first published or only when he sent them to us.

12313:
As promised, here are details the rest of the programs that I've been working on lately, which have now been uploaded to the FTP site. I've still been sticking with 300 baud, which probably comprises the majority of the tapes I still need to archive. I basically just chose the most interesting tapes from a few large collections  those originating from Brett Bilbrey, Richard Houser, and Bob Fabris. I'll try to note which collection each program came from, and also whether it looked like an official commercial tape.

In particular, I found many programs from George Moses, who didn't have many Bally BASIC programs archived before. In terms of pure numbers of programs, it's hard to beat the collection tapes 15 Two Part Inventions, Arcade Christmas Music, and Bally Arcade Ragtime. Those alone represent 56 programs. However, people will probably be more interested in the assorted music which as far as I know was never published. This varies from classical works like Fur Elise and the William Tell Overture to contemporary songs like Afternoon Delight, Take It Easy, and Hit The Road Jack.

I also found tapes of some old commercial programs that we at best had just had the source scans for, such as from John Collins and Robert Strand. There are also a number of unpublished Arcadian submissions by authors such as Jim Dunson and Larry Camnitz.

If you have time to watch it load, check out the Explorer I animation by A.R.D.

For some programs, I don't know the name and/or author. This particularly happened with programs in Brett's collection. If Brett or anyone else happens to remember something about these, please speak up.

There are a lot more details I could go over, but for that I'll just included the notes I took while archiving these.


A.R.D. / H.A.R.D.:
3x5 Character Set (1982)(H.A.R.D.)(300 baud)(PD).zip - archived from tape in Brett Bilbrey's collection.
A.R.D. Logo (1980)(A.R.D.)(300 baud)(PD).zip - archived from commercial Graphics Demo tape in Richard Houser's collection. This was the second program on side 2. Load with ":INPUT 2" and leave the recording running.
Arcadian Sampler (1980)(A.R.D.)(300 baud)(PD).zip - archived from tape in Bob Fabris' collection. This can replace the raw recording currently on-line.
Checkbook (1980)(A.R.D.)(300 baud)(PD).zip - archived from commercial tape in Richard Houser's collection. An identical version was also found in Bob Fabris' collection. Enter amounts as six-digit numbers, i.e. 050001 for $500.01. The program puts in the decimal point automatically. This can replace the raw recording currently on-line.
Decimal To Poke (1980)(A.R.D.)(300 baud)(PD).zip - archived from commercial Graphics Demo tape in Richard Houser's collection. This was the fourth program on side 1. Load with ":INPUT 4".
Explorer I (1980)(A.R.D.)(300 baud)(PD).zip - archived from commercial Graphics Demo tape in Richard Houser's collection. This was the first program on side 2. Load with ":INPUT 1" and leave the recording running.
Poke To Pixel Chart (1980)(A.R.D.)(300 baud)(PD).zip - archived from commercial Graphics Demo tape in Richard Houser's collection. This was the second program on side 1. Load with ":INPUT 2".

      As promised, here are details the rest of the programs that I've been working on lately, which have now been uploaded to the FTP site. I've still been sticking with 300 baud, which probably comprises the majority of the tapes I still need to archive. I basically just chose the most interesting tapes from a few large collections – those originating from Brett Bilbrey, Richard Houser, and Bob Fabris. I'll try to note which collection each program came from, and also whether it looked like an official commercial tape.



In particular, I found many programs from George Moses, who didn't have many Bally BASIC programs archived before. In terms of pure numbers of programs, it's hard to beat the collection tapes –15 Two Part Inventions, Arcade Christmas Music, and Bally Arcade Ragtime. Those alone represent 56 programs. However, people will probably be more interested in the assorted music which as far as I know was never published. This varies from classical works like Fur Elise and the William Tell Overture to contemporary songs like Afternoon Delight, Take It Easy, and Hit The Road Jack.



I also found tapes of some old commercial programs that we at best had just had the source scans for, such as from John Collins and Robert Strand. There are also a number of unpublished Arcadian submissions by authors such as Jim Dunson and Larry Camnitz.



If you have time to watch it load, check out the Explorer I animation by A.R.D.



For some programs, I don't know the name and/or author. This particularly happened with programs in Brett's collection. If Brett or anyone else happens to remember something about these, please speak up.



There are a lot more details I could go over, but for that I'll just included the notes I took while archiving these.

Enter amounts as six-digit numbers, i.e. 050001 for $500.01. The program puts in the decimal point automatically. This can replace the raw recording currently on-line.

> Life For Two (1978)(Joe Borrello)(300 baud).zip,
> Life For Two (19xx)(Joe Borrello and Brett Bilbrey)(300 baud).zip -
> archived from tape in Brett Bilbrey's collection. I'm not sure if the
> version Brett contributed to is a mod or a collaboration. It's a two player
> competition based on Life. In the first round, each player selects three
> squares in a grid to place a cell on. The available spaces light up one at
> a time, and only cycle through once. Pull the trigger on the desired
> squares to place the pieces. You can't see where the other player places
> them until the selecting is complete. Then the cells go through one
> reproduction cycle. In subsequent rounds, each player can place only one
> new cell. The game ends when a player has no cells left after the
> reproduction step. In the version by Joe Borrello alone, I often had
> trouble getting the program to recognize where I wanted to place cells.

Wow... That brought back some memories... Sadly, I don't recollect many details from that long ago... I'll try to add comments where possible.

I pack-ratted a lot of code back then, I also wrote a lot of code (both BASIC and assembler code).

I wrote a lot of enabling code to allow others to load data (like with George Moses and his music). And I wrote a bunch of programs with Joe Borrello just for fun. Joe had a lot of good ideas for programs, and I usually just helped with implementation issues...

I was inspired by many (Craig Anderson for example). I was particularly intrigued with his Electronic Ear. The 'ear' opened my eyes to looking at things with different perspectives...

I was also tickled by George's music, so that was why I collected so much of it. We had a LOT of fun. :-)

Also, I used to 'fix' or modify programs. So it does not surprise me that many of 'my' archived programs were 'slightly' different, but I could not tell you what those changes were... (well, not without going back and reverse engineering the changes.

"Hi" was indeed a letter from someone, but I don't remember what was in it.

I also helped teach a programmer that went on to code some early programs on the Mac. Ironically... ;-)

I 'think' that things like &(21) =VC were poking the internal sound drivers volume control. Tone C. Checking the nutting manual, page 106 shows the port numbers (in hex), so 21 dec is 15 hex.

As to ZZZ-UNK, I don't remember that name, but I wrote a lot of utilities to help me code the cartridges. My 'modus operandi' was to build tools to enable me doing things. (like the machine language loader for Music that George used so well)

I won't have time to go through things, or look at code, but I will try to answer questions if I can...

Brett

ZZZ-UNK is part of the TOSEC naming convention for when the a program's title is unknown. Nothing in the collection was actually labeled that way.  I believe I labeled two of the programs from your collection that way. They're both pretty short.

ZZZ-UNK (data entry) (19xx)(probably Spectre Systems)(300 baud):
  10 clear ;NT=0;B=0;:input
  20 A=KP;@(B)=A;B=B+1;goto 20
  30 clear ;NT=0;input "READY?"Z;:print
  40 for C=0to B+1;CY=0;CX=0;TV=@(C);next C;:return

ZZZ-UNK (number conversion) (19xx)(unknown author)(300 baud):
   3 .
   5 .
   7 :return
  10 print ;input B
  20 for I=1to 16;@(I)=0;next I
  30 A=%(B);C=ABS(A)
  40 for I=16to 1step -1
  50 C=Cdiv 2
  60 D=RM;@(I)=D
  70 if C=0goto 90
  80 next I;goto 100
  90 I=1;next I
 100 if A>-1goto 200
 110 for I=1to 16
 120 D=@(I);if D=1@(I)=0
 130 if D=0@(I)=1
 140 next I

 160 if @(I)=0@(I)=1;goto 180
 170 @(I)=0;next I;goto 200
 180 I=1;next I

 202 print " ",;for I=1to 8;print #1,@(I),;next I

 215 if I=9TV=32

 230 next K;if J<10TV=48+J
 240 if J>9TV=55+J

First, it was nice to see Craig answer that question that I put out there about if the animation is from the tutorial.  Thanks!

I have NOT re-read the tutorial in YEARS, but from memory I recall that the video is slow because it's streaming from the 300-baud tape.  That's the trick of the tutorial.  That is, you can have an animation as detailed and as long as you want, regardless of how little memory that your Astrocade has, just as long as you can follow these two rules/limits:

1) Speed - Streaming from 300-baud isn't fast... so neither is the animation.  To get "around" this, make an animation that doesn't need fast movement.  Which, kinda, sounds like a contradiction in terms.  Still, it works.

2) Length - The length of the animation is limited by how much data can be put on a tape.  So, a five-minute tape, common back in the 1970's and '80's to hold data, would have to have a MUCH shorter animation than a 90-minute tape.  Don't get the length of the tape confused for the length of the animation.  That is, a ten-minute tape does not equal a ten-minute animation.  I forget how it works, but once the main program is loaded that puts the data on-screen, then you're just loading the bytes on-screen and it just depends on what the constant rate is that the data streams from tape... or, in our case nowadays, from our PC... or Mac ;-)

Here's a link to the newsletter with the "Cursor" newsletter with Craig Anderson's tutorial, ""DMA Graphics" on pages 25-29:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/cursor/cursor_vol_1_issue_04.pdf

It's always nice to hear from folks from back in the day... you guys rock!

Adam

Life For Two (1978)(Joe Borrello)(300 baud).zip,

Life For Two (19xx)(Joe Borrello and Brett Bilbrey)(300 baud).zip - archived from tape in Brett Bilbrey's collection. I'm not sure if the version Brett contributed to is a mod or a collaboration. It's a two player competition based on Life. In the first round, each player selects three squares in a grid to place a cell on. The available spaces light up one at a time, and only cycle through once. Pull the trigger on the desired squares to place the pieces. You can't see where the other player places them until the selecting is complete. Then the cells go through one reproduction cycle. In subsequent rounds, each player can place only one new cell. The game ends when a player has no cells left after the reproduction step. In the version by Joe Borrello alone, I often had trouble getting the program to recognize where I wanted to place cells.

I'm not sure if the version Brett contributed to is a mod or a collaboration. It's a two player competition based on Life. In the first round, each player selects three squares in a grid to place a cell on. The available spaces light up one at a time, and only cycle through once. Pull the trigger on the desired squares to place the pieces. You can't see where the other player places them until the selecting is complete. Then the cells go through one reproduction cycle. In subsequent rounds, each player can place only one new cell. The game ends when a player has no cells left after the reproduction step. In the version by Joe Borrello alone, I often had trouble getting the program to recognize where I wanted to place cells.

>> > > Life For Two (19xx)(Joe Borrello and Brett Bilbrey)(300 baud).zip - archived from tape in Brett Bilbrey's collection. I'm not sure if the version Brett contributed to is a mod or a collaboration. It's a two player competition based on Life. In the first round, each player selects three squares in a grid to place a cell on. The available spaces light up one at a time, and only cycle through once. Pull the trigger on the desired squares to place the pieces. You can't see where the other player places them until the selecting is complete. Then the cells go through one reproduction cycle. In subsequent rounds, each player can place only one new cell. The game ends when a player has no cells left after the reproduction step. In the version by Joe Borrello alone, I often had trouble getting the program to recognize where I wanted to place cells.

    As promised, here are details the rest of the programs that I've been working on lately, which have now been uploaded to the FTP site. I've still been sticking with 300 baud, which probably comprises the majority of the tapes I still need to archive. I basically just chose the most interesting tapes from a few large collections – those originating from Brett Bilbrey, Richard Houser, and Bob Fabris. I'll try to note which collection each program came from, and also whether it looked like an official commercial tape.

    In particular, I found many programs from George Moses, who didn't have many Bally BASIC programs archived before. In terms of pure numbers of programs, it's hard to beat the collection tapes –15 Two Part Inventions, Arcade Christmas Music, and Bally Arcade Ragtime. Those alone represent 56 programs. This varies from classical works like Fur Elise and the William Tell Overture to contemporary songs like Afternoon Delight, Take It Easy, and Hit The Road Jack.

    As promised, here are details the rest of the programs that I've been 
    working on lately, which have now been uploaded to the FTP site. I've still 
    been sticking with 300 baud, which probably comprises the majority of the 
    tapes I still need to archive. I basically just chose the most interesting 
    tapes from a few large collections – those originating from Brett Bilbrey, 
    Richard Houser, and Bob Fabris. I'll try to note which collection each 
    program came from, and also whether it looked like an official commercial 
    tape.

In particular, I found many programs from George Moses, who 
    didn't have many Bally BASIC programs archived before. In terms of pure 
    numbers of programs, it's hard to beat the collection tapes –15 Two Part 
    Inventions, Arcade Christmas Music, and Bally Arcade Ragtime. Those alone 
    represent 56 programs. However, people will probably be more interested in 
    the assorted music which as far as I know was never published. This varies 
    from classical works like Fur Elise and the William Tell Overture to 
    contemporary songs like Afternoon Delight, Take It Easy, and Hit The Road 
    Jack.

I also found tapes of some old commercial programs that we at 
    best had just had the source scans for, such as from John Collins and Robert 
    Strand. There are also a number of unpublished Arcadian submissions by 
    authors such as Jim Dunson and Larry Camnitz.

If you have time to 
    watch it load, check out the Explorer I animation by A.R.D.

For some 
    programs, I don't know the name and/or author. This particularly happened 
    with programs in Brett's collection. If Brett or anyone else happens to 
    remember something about these, please speak up.

    available spaces light up one at a time, and only cycle through once. Pull

Hi everyone,

 Removing the top shield DOES allow for better air flow. However, some people don't know how to remove it safely, and as a result they inadvertently damage some component(s). For those that don't know how to do it, it would take a LOT of work.

To boil it down, the entire Bally/Astrocade PCB should be removed. This involves taking the top plastic off (5 screws), Taking the chassis out of the bottom plastic (4 screws) and then removing the Keyboard plastic CAREFULLY (4 more screws), because the keypad PCB is attached and needs to be removed by sliding it out. Then you need to separate the top shield from the bottom. This means taking as many as 8 clips off of it. Now you need to separate the main PCB from the bottom by removing the 5-10 screws holding them together. If, by chance, you have one of the original 1977 3164 boards, you might have a different scenario. They had a piece of cardboard covered with a metal film. These were put on the bottom of the PCB with push-in snaps. THOSE are very tricky to remove.
When you have the metal chassis and the RF shield separated, you can either cut or carefully bend the top shield up and down to remove, or unsolder them. It will take either a BIG soldering iron or a small propane torch to separate them this way.
Now that the parts of the separated, you need to reassemble the entire unit. Be careful to place the nylon washer on the screw that is next to the RESET button, and all of the lock washers on the remaining PCB to chassis screws.
when all is said and done (carefully) your unit should last longer. There are no guarantees because the parts in the units are all over 33 years old.

As far as a fan underneath, the circulating air in the unit will help keep it cooler. it goes into the bottom, swirls around inside and leaves via the vent holes in the cartridge storage area, the cassette area and any small area of venteng via the hand control area.

confused yet?

Ken

I added the "Bally BASIC Hexadecimal/Decimal Conversion Process" tutorial by Adam Trionfo (that's me!) to BallyAlley.com.

This short tutorial explains how to convert from Bally and AstroBASIC hex format to decimal and vice versa. Normally this process can be handled swiftly with a calculator that can simply convert decimal and hex values, but this is not the case with Bally BASIC.  This conversion process relies on, and builds upon methods discussed in 1982's Bally Arcade/Astrocade booklet called "Z-80 Mini Course" by Larry Simioni.

This conversion process was first discussed on the Bally Alley discussion board on May 21 and 22, 2013.  It seems useful to have this information easily accessible on BallyAlley.com, so I've made a short tutorial using what I already wrote.  In this tutorial I'm not trying to explain the basics of hex.  If you understand hex already and are are wondering why the decimal values in Bally BASIC are not what you expect them to be when converted to hex using a calculator, then this tutorial will set you straight.

You can read the tutorial here:

http://tinyurl.com/kkyc7lf

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.ballyalley.com/basic/Bally%20BASIC%20Hex%20Conversion%20(2013)(Adam%20Trionfo).txt

Thanks to Paul for coaxing this out of me a week or so ago.  Writing this helped to set ME straight on what's going on!

Have fun!

Adam

Video Rally (which I wanted to call Bally Rally but decided against it for good reasons) was written for a Twin City Rally Club Christmas Party in 1979 or 1980. It's fairly esoteric in its use of the "Main Road Rule" that was popular in TSD rallying back then, and has a bug that allows cheating once you discover it. I never got around to fixing it but the game was the hit of the party for a couple of years. You DO need the instructions if you weren't on the rally circuit in the late 70s, early 80s.

Craig Anderson

After uploading to BallyAlley all of those 300-Baud, Bally BASIC songs by George Moses yesterday, I had thoughts of three-tone music dancing around my head.  I asked my son, Dominic (freshmen in college who is majoring in music education), to write a short jazz piece of about 30 seconds.  I thought that I'd convert it for play on the Astrocade using the program that George Moses and Brett Bilbrey wrote (and which George used for his music releases).  I wasn't sure if he'd get around to making the song or not, but I told him it had to be three voices.  That's the only limit that I gave to him other than song length.  I probably should have said something about length of notes too.  I didn't REALLY expect him to run with this idea.

About an hour and a half later my son calls me into his room to listen to him completed 40-second song, which he calls "Astrocade Jam."  Man, I can't imagine how he wrote that so fast.  It would take me a LONG time to get this song into the Astrocade-- if ever!  So, I got his permission to share the song with all of you.

Attached to this posting (technically, online at the Yahoo Groups) are:

1) Astrocade Jam.pdf - The three pages of sheet music composed using Finale.

2) Astrocade Jam.mp3 - An version of the song output from Finale.

I hope that you like the song.  Maybe I'll figure out how to make something like this work on the Astrocade.  Maybe I'll have to work with the composer and whittle it down a bit, you know, to MY level!

Oh, Brett, if you have any swing over that at Apple maybe he can write an ipad jingle... ;-)

Enjoy!

      With the help of Richard Houser's Arcadian compilation tapes borrowed from Lance, I've been able to really thoroughly archive the first two volumes of The Arcadian. This was before AstroBASIC was even out, so you'd better like 300 baud! Richard's tapes covered the first couple of volumes pretty thoroughly. He included all of the big programs, but didn't always put in small programs or variations of longer programs. But once I had these, it was pretty easy to generate the alternative versions (as when Bob printed a reader suggestion for improving a program). And the short programs I just typed in and converted with the 300 baud tools for the PC.  Sometimes, Richard made small changes to the code printed in The Arcadian. I won't guarantee I caught all of these, but when I did, I've included both his modified version and the original.  The tape for volume 3 had only a small portion of the programs from this volume. As far as I know, this is all he did. I'm including all the programs from this tape that hadn't already been archived, but I haven't tried to fill in the gaps.



Here's a list of what I uploaded to the FTP server (dated 5-23-2013). I haven't made notes for most of the programs, because the best source of information is probably looking them up in The Arcadian. Check Mike White's software list to find the exact locations. If I have a version of a program with comments removed, it's because the program ran out of memory as it was printed. I'm not sure why they included comment lines in this case.  A few programs require a RAM expansion, but they still just load into Bally BASIC with :INPUT.  I discovered that the Critter program we got from Mike White included some of his own modifications. I'm not sure if these were made when Critter was first published or only when he sent them to us.

12381:
All of the expanded BASICs require a memory unit attached to the 50 pin connector on the back of the unit. The 50 pin connector has all of the address lines (A0-A15) as well as write and read lines and more.
The cartridge slot has only 8 data lines and address lines A0-A12.
Both Bally and Astro BASIC cartridges can only access 23768 bytes. If you go9 over that, the BASIC sees it as a negative number. They cannot interpret the negative numbers as addresses. It's just not in the code.
Addresses A0 through A12 total $3FFF

I hope this helps
Ken

12385:
When Jay (now Jamie) wrote the 1st 2 BASICS, there didn't seem to be any need for more than $4FFF of any memory. He did however leave an access to $7FFF. when he wrote the Hot Rod BASIC he changed the code. It no longer does any pixel sharing (a method used to save memory which was very expensive at the time) so it was faster, and had more access. As long as there is data that can go to the Z80, the addresses can be accessed through the 50 pin. There is not any basic write or read functions available in the cartridge slot. There is only a chip select, the address lines A0-A12 and the data lines D0-D7, power and ground (3) a total of 26 pins, but only 25 are actually used.
Ken

12386:
Yes, clearly a cartridge CAN access the expanded RAM, because I have done it myself with a cartridge version of Blue RAM BASIC 1.1. I've also played WaveMakers expanded RAM games from the multi-cart. Obviously, any such cartridge would be limiting its potential audience, since not that many people have RAM expansions, but that's the only down-side I can think of.

As Ken said, even Bally BASIC and AstroBASIC can access part of the expanded RAM, and the fact that they can't access it all is merely because they weren't programmed to do so.

Perhaps there's some confusion as to what bank-switching would do.  If I recall correctly, the Astrocade's address space allocates 8K to the cartridge. That's the read only memory (ROM) space that it reads the data on the cartridge from. The program on the cartridge is then free to utilize any of the random access memory (RAM) to do it's calculations by reading from it or writing to it, including the memory in the RAM expansion. Ordinarily, you couldn't have a cartridge larger than 8K, but if you use bank-switching, you can change around which parts of the cartridge ROM are in the Astrocade's ROM address space at any particular time. So, for example, you could make unique sprites for each level of a game. This could be done with or without a RAM expansion.

Paul

12394:
The discussion reminded me that I wrote up an explanation of the Astrocade address space for MESS.  Perhaps the extra details will be useful.

The R&L expansion actually does allow you to remap some or all of the cartridge address space as RAM instead of ROM, though this RAM would still be physically on the expansion board, not the cartridge.

/*************************************
 *
 *  Memory maps
 *
 * $0000 to $1FFF:  8K on-board ROM (could be one of three available BIOS dumps)
 * $2000 to $3FFF:  8K cartridge ROM
 * $4000 to $4FFF:  4K screen RAM
 * $5000 to $FFFF:  44K address space not available in standard machine.  With a
 * sufficiently large RAM expansion, all of this RAM can be added, and accessed
 * by an extended BASIC program.  Bally and Astrocade BASIC can access from
 * $5000 to $7FFF if available.

 *  RAM Expansions
 *
 * Several third party RAM expansions have been made for the Astrocade.  These
 * allow access to various ranges of the expansion memory ($5000 to $FFFF).
 * A RAM expansion is required to use extended BASIC programs like Blue RAM BASIC
 * and VIPERSoft BASIC.  All of the expansions also have a RAM protect switch, which
 * can be flipped at any time to make the RAM act like ROM.  Extended BASIC
 * programs need access to the RAM and won't work with RAM protect enabled, but
 * this can be useful with Bally and Astrocade BASIC.  They also have a range switch
 * (not implemented).  The default position is 6K, but it can be switched to
 * 2K.  This means that the expanded memory starting at $6000 will instead be
 * mapped to the cartridge memory starting at $2000.  So it would be possible to
 * load a cartridge program from tape into the expansion memory, then flip the range
 * switch and run it as a cartridge.  This is useful for cartridge development.
 *
 * NOTE:  If you have any trouble running cartridges with a RAM expansion installed, hit reset.
 *
 * Blue RAM -- available in 4K, 16K, and 32K.  These also use an INS8154 chip,
 * (not yet implemented) which has an additional $80 bytes of RAM mapped
 * immediately after the end of the expansion address space.  This memory
 * can't be write protected.  The INS8154 has I/O features needed for loading
 * tape programs into Blue RAM BASIC, as well as running the Blue RAM Utility cart.
 * 4K:  $6000 to $6FFF (can't run VIPERSoft BASIC, because this program needs memory
 * past this range)
 * 16K:  $6000 to $9FFF
 * 32K:  $6000 to $DFFF
 *
 * VIPER System 1 -- This is available in 16K only.  It also includes a keyboard (not implemented).
 * 16K:  $6000 to $9FFF
 *
 * Lil' WHITE RAM -- This is available in 32K only.  Attempts to read and write
 * to memory outside of its address range ($D000 to $FFFF) are mapped to the expansion
 * memory $5000 to $7FFF.  The current implementation won't allow the shadow RAM area
 * to be accessed when RAM protect is on, but there is no known software that will
 * access the upper range of the expansion RAM when RAM protect is enabled.
 * 32K:  $5000 to $CFFF
 *
 * R&L 64K RAM Board -- This is a highly configurable kit.  RAM can be installed in
 * 2K increments.  So, the entire 44K expansion memory can be filled.  It is also
 * possible to override the rest of the memory map with RAM (not implemented).
 * There are 32 switches allowing users to activate and deactivate each 2K block (not implemented).
 * RAM write protection can be implemented in three ranges through jumpers or by
 * installing switches.  The ranges are $0000 to $0FFF (first 4K), $0000 to $3FFF (first 16K),

 * $5000 to $FFFF, with only a single write protect covering this entire range.

Yes, clearly a cartridge CAN access the expanded RAM, because I have done it myself with a cartridge version of Blue RAM BASIC 1.1. I've also played WaveMakers expanded RAM games from the multi-cart. Obviously, any such cartridge would be limiting its potential audience, since not that many people have RAM expansions, but that's the only down-side I can think of. As Ken said, even Bally BASIC and AstroBASIC can access part of the expanded RAM, and the fact that they can't access it all is merely because they weren't programmed to do so. Perhaps there's some confusion as to what bank-switching would do.  If I recall correctly, the Astrocade's address space allocates 8K to the cartridge. That's the read only memory (ROM) space that it reads the data on the cartridge from. The program on the cartridge is then free to utilize any of the random access memory (RAM) to do it's calculations by reading from it or writing to it, including the memory in the RAM
 expansion. Ordinarily, you couldn't have a cartridge larger than 8K, but if you use bank-switching, you can change around which parts of the cartridge ROM are in the Astrocade's ROM address space at any particular time. So, for example, you could make unique sprites for each level of a game. This could be done with or without a RAM expansion. Paul
