12400:
I'm a little late to the party here, as it seems that the cart RAM question has already been answered quite well to Micheal's satisfaction.  Here's what's been established:

1) Extra RAM can not go, physically, into the same space as the cartridge port.  That is, there is no way to write to RAM there.

2) All machine language carts can access all RAM, whether built-into the Astrocade, external to the unit (Blue Ram, for example) or both.

3) Bally BASIC, AstroBASIC and Color BASIC can NOT access RAM outside of the internal RAM of the unit when running pure BASIC code.

4) There is a work-around for BB, AB, and CB that lets these BASIC's access the external RAM, but it requires machine language code routines to be written, or at least USED, by the programmer.  As Ken has emphasized, these earlier BASICs were not created to access more than 4K of RAM.

5) Blue Ram and Vipersoft BASIC can access external RAM.

6) While a properly written program on cartridge CAN access external RAM, say all of the 32K of the Lil' White Ram, doing so would limit the audience to handful of people.  So, for instance, 52 carts of "Crazy Climber" were sold.  If "Crazy Climber" had used external memory, than only those people with a RAM expansion could play the game.

7) An Astrocade cartridge is STILL limited to 8K of ROM.  The size of the program all still needs to be squeezed into the same amount of space as was available to Astrocade games in 1982.  For instance, the early 1980's "The Incredible Wizard" was an 8K game.  That amount of ROM programming 8,192 bytes) is still all that any Astrocade cartridge programmer has to work with today.

8) A Bankswitched cart can hold more than 8K of ROM.  For instance, a 512K bankswitched cart for the Astrocade has this memory map:

http://www.bally128k.com/maxflash/Astrocade_Maxflash_512K_Memory_Map.txt

9) Bankswitched carts are not supported in the Astrocade's MESS emulation.  Thus, it's more difficult to program these devices.

Have I summed up this conversation thus far?

So, Michael, what's the phone call that you had to make all about?!?

12404:
Well, the way I was designing it, it would have been on two systems in the same room (connected to each other via their expansion ports).

But... The game 'theoretically could be played' through phone lines. The only issue would be the latency of the phone interface affecting the speed of the game play. (But I did not think about a 'dial up' solution back then.)



And with respect to the other discussion about RAM in the cartridge port, I did design a system with a TRS-80 that 'mapped' the cartridge addressing space into the TRS-80 expansion RAM unit. (The TRS-80 'RAM' appeared as a cartridge to the Z80 in the Bally.)

The TRS-80 could change data in the 'cartridge space' on the fly to facilitate debugging games. (The Bally could just read the data, not write any.) I felt this was more powerful than the UV-1 Datamax systems that Bally and Action Graphics used for developing cartridges.

12418:
Well, it was a long day guys when I made that post, a little bit fact, a little bit fiction, but I'm sure you guys had a laugh or two.
 
The reality is, we really do have a working bank-switching board for the Astrocade.  Four of them to be exact, which were prototypes I had Steve make.  They were originally configured with 256k of ROM when we first tested them, and now two have been fitted with 512k. 
 
The hasn't been too much progress recently due to many of us having other commitments and just plain daily life duties in general, but I'm working on getting the 128kgames.com site up and running with at least photos of the boards and possibly some video of them in action. 
 
My goal originally was to fund and actually publish some incredible games for the system from that site, which is something I still hope to accomplish.  But we still have some obstacles to overcome, the least of which is getting the new board supported in Mess.  
 
Ideally, it would be great to have our own dedicated Astrocade emulator, like so many other platforms have, with support for the board and expanded RAM in various configurations.  This I believe would make it much easier for programmers to build and test their work.
 
I'd like to open up the entire project to everyone and make all the data and specifications available.  I'm hoping to drum up interest in the community which might lead to some significant breakthroughs.   I've also got two other domains with basic hosting options which could be used for a dedicated forum or additional file hosting (we're currently using one to host files for the cart). 
 
In the meantime if anyone wants to have a look around at the files, you can access the site from here:
 
bally128k.com
 
If anyone is interested in reading up on the development process just send me an email and I'll add you to the Google group "The 128k Project" which details everything.
 
-Michael

Some quick comments for those not in the know about this software.  The three programs mentioned by Paul require the Blue Ram Unit.  The products themselves (well, the cables for the products) insert into the ZIF socket.

1) 300 baud
modem - A serial modem could be connected to the Blue Ram.  I'm guessing that a faster one could be used with the hardware, but there is no software to support it.  I can't remember if the modem software is Hayes compatible or not.  If
so, then it should work with any generic Hayes-compatible 300-Baud
modem.  Heck, it would even would with a 56K modem... at 300-Baud
rates... ;-)


2) BSR - The software would allow communication with the BSR X-10 Ultrasonic Remote Control System.  Allows the user to control up to 16 lights or appliances.  Interestingly, the X-10 standard is still in use to this day for communication with home automation devices!

3) EEPROM drivers - An EPROM (not EEPROM) burner could be connected to the Blue Ram.  Only a handful of these devices were made, but they saw heavy use by those that owned them like Mike White for the creation of MANY carts and I think that Ken Lill still may even use his burner to this day.

I'm not sure how to check this software-- though I guess Ken (or Mike?) could test the EPROM burning software.  My recommendation would be to digitally archive the software to the best that can be tested, but still distribute the non-digitally archived version just in case it's broken in some way.

These are highly specialized programs for hardware that VERY few people have.  Those with the hardware wouldn't find much use for it.  I'm not saying that the program shouldn't be archived (that would completely defeat the purpose of digital archiving), but that it will be very difficult to find anyone to TEST the programs.

Good luck testing the programs, Paul.  The amount of effort that you put into archiving for the little-'ol Bally is simply amazing!

Adam

Attached are the Z80 disassembly and ML listing for the "Blue RAM Modem Controller."  This is as far as I'm going to take the source code of the modem driver (which is, really, just a start... but it is a heck of a lot further along than it was yesterday morning!).  Hopefully Ken can take the code for these programs to the show with him.  However, I think that part of the original point of this was to see if this was legit code-- and it obviously is Z80 code that runs in the correct area and accessed areas of Astrocade memory that ought to be accessed.  So, maybe that's all the code NEEDS to be taken.

There are a few iffy areas of this driver (jp $6ee8 is also off by a byte, as I've already described: it jumps into the middle of a mnemonic starting at address $6EE7).  Also, I think that one area must be data (12 bytes starting at $6EF4), so I marked these bytes with Define Bytes.  If that area is code, then the program doesn't Jump or CALL it, nor does the BASIC program seem to access it either.  That doesn't mean there isn't another way into that area... just not an east-to-see method.  You'll discover that if you DO disassemble that portion of the program that it makes a call about the joysticks... which makes no sense to me.

I'm going to place the disassembly and ML listing in this posting, for reference (and I'm going to post this as "plain text" to see if that helps with the formatting), but it will probably be much easier to read the attached files: modem.asm and modem.lst.  Plus, it will be easier to just pick up these files and use them.

Thanks for bringing this to the group, Paul.  It was a fun little diversion.

Have fun with it, guys!

Adam

12478:
One thing to remember about mixed programs (ML & BASIC) is that all of the BASIC programs use the DE register pair to save the location of where to return to in BASIC once done with the ML code.


In the BASIC program the variable M is not set, but is used. This means that it is either set by the ML or it is preloaded and saved on the recording.

The Register pair DE is the marker for where the BASIC program is. The first thing you should do (as good practice) is to PUSH DE then just before you return to BASIC you need to POP DE  then RETurn.
The only other way to return if you use the DE pair in your program is to put the number into the STACK that corresponds to where you want to RETurn. If you alter your BASIC program before that address.... never never land !

> but when Paul archived the program he credits Rich Tietjens too. Paul, can
> you give some details about this?
>
> Instructions from the "Arcadian:"
>
> BIORYTHM by Dave Walter is a version that stores the data for the three
> graphs outside the program in string locations, and then directs their
> printing in the proper place on the screen. The sine wave is therefore
> quite accurately portrayed. In addition, it is fast moving. To load the
> string data, load this on tape and save before the program is manually
> loaded:
>
> 10 FOR A=0 TO 86
> 20 PRINT #1 ,"@(",A,")=",
> 30 INPUT @(A)
> 40 NEXT A
>
> After punching in the program, load the string from the tape. The program is
> now complete. Dump to tape as follows:
>
> :PRINT;LIST;FOR A=0 TO 86;PRINT #1, "@(",A,")=", @(A); NEXT A; PRINT"
> CLEAR;RUN
>
> Then load back to Bally and the program will be self starting.
>
> "Bio-rhythms" has no instructions, but I have gathered this information from
> the BASIC listing:
>
> The program will ask for the current date and also your birth date. I
> didn't notice anything else being asked for. Based on this information the
> programs tells you:
>
> 1) How long you have lived.
> 2) Physical Index.
> 3) Emotional Index.
> 4) Intellectual Index.
>
> I have no idea what this represents, but these types of programs were very
> popular (at least to write and publish) in the 1970's, and I suppose that it
> was presumed the user would know what to do with this information. Perhaps
> break up a date for the evening? Maybe fly off to Vegas and get married?
> Decide this week looks good to have a kid. It was up to the user to decide
> what to do with the data-- and I'm sure that the programmer couldn't be held
> accountable for any poor life choices based on some simple numbers.
>
> I noticed that when the program loads and before it begins that the user
> gets this message:
>
> WARNING.......
> ANY ATTEMPT to CHANGE
> THIS PROGRAM WILL CAUSE
> THE GRAPHICS to
>
> SELF-DESTRUCT
>
> THIS PROGRAM WILL BE

> BIO-RYTHYMS IN 3 MINS.
